What is on record is the yardstick that growth would be read against. Revenue compounded at {earnings_versus_cash.history.revenue_growth_three_year_compound|pct} a year over three fiscal years and {earnings_versus_cash.history.revenue_growth_five_year_compound|pct} over five, then grew {ratios.growth.revenue.trailing_four_quarters|pct} over the trailing four quarters and {ratios.growth.revenue.year_over_year|pct} in the latest quarter against the year-earlier quarter. Management's outlook is directional rather than a long-run number: MD&A says "we anticipate significant ISG and strong CSG net revenue growth", the release says the AI server business "exited the quarter with a record $95 billion backlog", and its outlook table for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 guides revenue up on the year-earlier quarter. The release does not define that backlog, and the accounting analysis could not tie it to remaining performance obligations. Against that record my base case sets year-one growth below the run rate the backlog and the guided quarter point to, and fades it to a terminal rate below both compound rates; whether the price asks for more or less than that cannot be said until a price series and a WACC are supplied.

most_sensitive.assumption: year-one revenue growth and its straight-line fade to the terminal rate
most_sensitive.reading: The sensitivity grid was not computed, because it runs on the WACC that is missing, so no sensitivity of value is read off it here. Of my own inputs, year-one revenue growth is where the three scenarios lie furthest apart: the bear case sits just above the five-year compound growth of {earnings_versus_cash.history.revenue_growth_five_year_compound|pct}, while the bull case sits much closer to, but still well below, the trailing-four-quarter growth of {ratios.growth.revenue.trailing_four_quarters|pct}. Python fades that rate in a straight line to the terminal rate over ten years, so the gap between cases carries into the size of the revenue base in every later year, which is why it is the first driver to test once a WACC exists. The record shows the gap is not idle: revenue changed by {earnings_versus_cash.history.years.2.revenue_growth|pct} in fiscal 2024, two years after growing {earnings_versus_cash.history.years.4.revenue_growth|pct} in fiscal 2022, and a single customer was {concentration.facts.0.value|pct} of fiscal 2026 revenue.

most_sensitive.reading: The second widest spread among my drivers is the operating margin path, which sets after-tax operating income in every year before reinvestment is taken out. The bear case returns year-ten margin close to fiscal 2024's {earnings_versus_cash.history.years.2.operating_margin|pct}, below the three-year average of {earnings_versus_cash.history.operating_margin_three_year_average|pct}, while the bull case keeps year-ten margin above the trailing {ratios.profitability.operating_margin|pct}, which no full year in the record has reached. The quarters show how quickly the underlying gross margin moves: it fell to {trend_table.quarters-back-1.ratios.gross_margin|pct} in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 and recovered to {trend_table.quarters-back-0.ratios.gross_margin|pct} in the second, which MD&A credits to pricing against "substantial inflation in memory component costs". The discount rate itself is a further open input rather than a ranked one: with no beta, the cost of equity and the WACC are unset, so how value moves with them cannot be read either.
